messages.content: I want to infer spatial conductivity and an unknown boundary flux from sparse temperature observations, while preserving uncertainty when the two are not identifiable. How should I understand the goal?

There are two linked aims: recover information about both the spatial conductivity and the boundary flux from the temperature observations, and represent what those observations cannot determine. If different conductivity–flux combinations remain consistent with sparse observations, the inference should not present one combination as uniquely established.
So preserving uncertainty is part of the goal, not just a qualification on the reconstruction?

Yes. The aim is not merely to produce estimates and then acknowledge uncertainty in words. The reported intervals for conductivity and flux should reflect uncertainty, including where joint recovery is nonidentifiable. The goal does not say that uncertainty must disappear; it says it must be preserved rather than concealed.
What is the numerical requirement for those intervals?

The target is 90% interval coverage, within five percentage points, for both conductivity and flux across identifiability regimes. Read literally, that permits coverage from 85% to 95% around the 90% target. The five-percentage-point allowance applies to coverage, not to the reconstructed parameter values.
Does that mean conductivity coverage alone could meet the target while flux coverage does not?

No. The requirement names both quantities. An assessment that only establishes the coverage target for conductivity would leave the flux requirement unaddressed, and the reverse is also true. The wording does not specify whether the intervals must have simultaneous coverage of conductivity and flux; it does explicitly require coverage for each.
And what does “across identifiability regimes” add?

It means the coverage aim is not confined to circumstances where joint recovery is straightforward. It also matters where the observations do not clearly distinguish conductivity from boundary flux. The requirement does not specify a list of regimes or a particular way to evaluate them, so those details should not be presumed.
Would it be inconsistent for the intervals to get wider in a less identifiable regime?

Not by itself. Less identifiable quantities can warrant more uncertainty. The stated coverage target does not require equally narrow intervals in every regime, and preserving uncertainty under nonidentifiability may call for intervals that reflect that ambiguity. No numerical interval-width target is given here.
Could a pair of precise-looking estimates still satisfy the goal if they fit the sparse temperature observations?

A fit to the observations would not, on its own, establish the uncertainty requirement. The goal concerns what can be inferred about conductivity and flux, not only whether one proposed pair is compatible with the observed temperatures. If the observations leave those quantities ambiguous, precise-looking estimates should not be treated as resolving that ambiguity without support.
There is also a reconstruction-error comparison. What exactly is being compared?

When joint recovery is identifiable, the conductivity reconstruction error should match the conductivity reconstruction error for a known-flux case within 20%. The known-flux error is the comparison baseline. This requirement compares conductivity reconstruction error; it does not state a corresponding 20% error comparison for the recovered flux.
Is the 20% an absolute error allowance?

It is phrased as being within 20% of the known-flux conductivity reconstruction error, so it is a relative comparison to that baseline, not a specified absolute error value. For example, the condition is about how far the joint-recovery error departs from the known-flux error relative to that reference. The goal does not provide either error numerically.
Does that comparison apply even when conductivity and flux cannot be identified jointly?

The stated condition is narrower: match the known-flux conductivity reconstruction error within 20% when joint recovery is identifiable. It does not impose that same reconstruction-error comparison on nonidentifiable cases. Those cases remain within the broader goal of representing uncertainty and the stated interval-coverage requirement.
I want to make sure the two numerical targets are not being blended together.

They measure different things. The 90% target, with a five-percentage-point tolerance, concerns interval coverage for conductivity and flux across identifiability regimes. The within-20% condition concerns conductivity reconstruction error relative to the known-flux baseline, specifically when joint recovery is identifiable. Meeting one condition would not, by itself, establish the other.
If coverage is 90%, should I describe every interval as having captured the true value?

No. Coverage is a performance target for intervals over the cases on which coverage is assessed, not a claim that every individual interval contains the true quantity. Nor does the target alone specify how to construct the intervals or how to assess coverage. It specifies the desired coverage level and tolerance.
Could I say the objective is simply to recover conductivity, with boundary flux treated as incidental?

That would leave out part of the objective. The boundary flux is unknown and is itself to be inferred from the sparse temperature observations. It also has its own interval-coverage requirement. The known-flux case appears as the baseline for the conditional conductivity-error comparison, not as a replacement for the unknown-flux inference goal.
Does the goal commit us to a particular inference method for handling nonidentifiability?

No method is specified. The goal states what should be inferred and how success should be judged, while leaving the means open. Whatever approach is used, it needs to avoid understating uncertainty when conductivity and flux cannot be distinguished well from the available observations.

Can I restate it as two demands: calibrated uncertainty throughout the identifiability range, and little loss in conductivity reconstruction compared with known flux where joint inference is possible?

That captures the distinction, provided the numerical conditions stay explicit: 90% interval coverage within five percentage points for both conductivity and flux across identifiability regimes, and conductivity reconstruction error within 20% of the known-flux error when joint recovery is identifiable. “Little loss” alone would be less precise than the stated comparison.
What approach would you propose for the conductivity and unknown-flux problem?

A proposed approach is hierarchical Bayesian heat-equation inversion. Represent the spatial log-conductivity with a Gaussian process, represent the unknown boundary flux with a spline, and use joint MCMC sampling to obtain posterior intervals for conductivity and flux. This describes an approach to the inference problem, not a claim that it has achieved the stated performance targets.
What makes it an inversion of the heat equation?

The heat equation relates conductivity and boundary flux to temperature. In an inverse problem, the direction of inference runs from the available temperature observations back toward those unknown quantities. Here both conductivity and flux are unknown, so they are inferred together rather than treating the flux as given.
Why put the Gaussian process on log-conductivity rather than directly on conductivity?

The proposal places the Gaussian-process model on the spatial *log*-conductivity. Conductivity is then obtained by transforming that latent field back from the log scale, which keeps the represented conductivity positive. It does not mean that conductivity itself has a Gaussian-process distribution on its original scale.
Does the Gaussian process say the true conductivity has to be a random function?

It is a probabilistic model for inference, not a claim that the physical conductivity is generated at random. The Gaussian process expresses prior uncertainty about the spatial log-conductivity and provides a way to relate uncertainty across locations. The observations can then update that uncertainty through the inversion.
And what role does the spline play for the boundary flux?

It supplies a representation for an unknown boundary flux using spline coefficients. Rather than assuming the flux is known, the inversion includes those coefficients among the unknowns. The proposal does not specify the spline's degree, knots, or other details, so it does not yet settle how flexible that representation would be.
Is calling the approach hierarchical the same as saying the spline coefficients have a particular prior?

No. “Hierarchical Bayesian” indicates a probabilistic structure connecting the unknown quantities, their prior descriptions, and the temperature observations. The proposal names a Gaussian-process model for log-conductivity and a spline representation for flux, but it does not specify a particular prior distribution for the spline coefficients or the details of any hyperparameters.
Why emphasize *joint* MCMC rather than getting an interval for each quantity independently?

Because conductivity and boundary flux can be related in what the temperature observations imply. Joint MCMC aims to sample their combined posterior distribution, retaining how plausible conductivity values pair with plausible flux values. Marginal posterior intervals for each can then be obtained without first pretending that the other unknown is fixed or independently determined.
Could the joint posterior show that several conductivity–flux combinations remain plausible?

Yes. That is one reason to use a joint uncertainty representation. If sparse temperature observations do not distinguish certain combinations well, the posterior can retain uncertainty along those combinations instead of reducing the result to a single conductivity field and a single flux estimate. How faithfully it does so still depends on the model and the resulting inference.
When you say “posterior intervals,” are they intervals around the MCMC averages?

Not necessarily. The proposal is to use joint MCMC to obtain intervals from the posterior distribution; it does not prescribe an interval construction or require centering them on an MCMC average. The important distinction is that the intervals represent uncertainty under the joint Bayesian model, rather than merely displaying one fitted result.
Does running MCMC guarantee that those intervals have the coverage target we discussed?

No. MCMC is a way to approximate the posterior described by the model; it does not itself guarantee a particular coverage rate. Posterior intervals and an assessed coverage target are related but distinct. The proposal specifies the inference approach, not evidence that its intervals meet the target.
Would the log-conductivity Gaussian process automatically solve nonidentifiability?

No. A prior can structure uncertainty, but it cannot make sparse observations distinguish conductivity from flux if the information is not there. A central concern is whether the joint posterior honestly retains ambiguity rather than allowing modeling assumptions to make the result appear more certain than the observations warrant.
Could a narrow posterior interval therefore be misleading?

It could be, if its narrowness came mainly from restrictive modeling assumptions rather than information in the observations. Narrow intervals are not inherently wrong, but the proposal alone gives no basis for claiming they are warranted. In a nonidentifiable setting, it is particularly important not to confuse posterior concentration under a model with independent evidence that the unknowns have been resolved.
Does the proposal require fitting conductivity first and flux second?

No. Its defining feature here is *joint* inference: the log-conductivity representation and the spline flux representation enter the heat-equation inversion together, and MCMC targets their joint posterior. The proposal does not prescribe a sequential fitting procedure.
If I describe it in one sentence, what should I keep explicit?

Keep all three modeling and inference elements: hierarchical Bayesian inversion of the heat equation, a Gaussian process for spatial log-conductivity, and a spline representation for the unknown boundary flux, with joint MCMC used to obtain posterior intervals. That wording preserves that both unknowns are inferred and that uncertainty about them is handled jointly, without claiming a result that has not been established.
How can joint posterior inference maintain calibrated intervals for conductivity and boundary flux when sparse temperature observations leave their sensitivities nearly collinear?

Near-collinear sensitivities mean that changes in conductivity and changes in boundary flux can produce very similar effects in the available temperature observations. Joint inference can retain that trade-off in the posterior instead of treating either unknown as fixed while estimating the other. Intervals derived from that posterior can then reflect the resulting ambiguity. But joint inference alone does not guarantee calibrated coverage; that also depends on whether the model and posterior intervals represent the relevant uncertainty adequately.
What does “nearly collinear” mean here without assuming the two unknowns are exactly indistinguishable?

It means the observed temperatures respond to certain changes in conductivity and flux in almost the same pattern. The observations may still distinguish those changes to some extent, but only weakly. The question is therefore about limited separation of their effects, not necessarily complete nonidentifiability.
Why is estimating them together better suited to that situation than estimating each in isolation?

If one quantity is held fixed, the inferred uncertainty in the other need not reflect uncertainty about the fixed quantity. A joint posterior instead represents plausible conductivity–flux combinations. When the temperature observations allow one quantity to change while the other changes correspondingly, that relationship remains part of the inference.
So should I picture the joint posterior as extended along a trade-off between them?

That is a useful conceptual picture. Near-collinear sensitivities can leave a range of combinations with similar implications for the sparse observations, making the posterior less concentrated in that direction. It is only an illustration, though: the question does not specify the shape of the posterior or the direction of the trade-off.
If the joint posterior shows the trade-off, will the separate conductivity and flux intervals necessarily be wide?

Not necessarily by a specified amount. Marginal intervals reflect the range of each quantity after accounting for the other, so a substantial unresolved trade-off can broaden them. Their actual widths also depend on the observations and the probabilistic model. The key point is that the intervals should not become artificially precise simply because the other unknown was treated as known.
Can the temperatures constrain something about the pair even if they constrain each member poorly?

Conceptually, yes. Observations can be more informative about a combined effect than about how much of that effect comes from conductivity versus flux. In that case, uncertainty about each separate quantity remains important even though some aspect of their combined influence is constrained. The question does not specify which combinations, if any, are well determined.
How does the proposed Bayesian model enter this question?

The proposed hierarchical heat-equation inversion places a Gaussian-process model on spatial log-conductivity and represents the unknown boundary flux with a spline. Joint MCMC is proposed to obtain posterior intervals while keeping both sets of unknowns in the same inference. The calibration question asks whether those intervals remain reliable when the observations weakly distinguish the two contributions; the proposed model by itself does not answer that question.
Could the Gaussian-process and spline representations hide the lack of identifiability?

They could influence how much uncertainty the posterior displays. Those representations supply structure beyond what the sparse temperatures alone provide. If that structure is restrictive, the posterior might appear precise even where the observations offer little separation. Conversely, allowing uncertainty in both unknowns gives the joint posterior a way to express ambiguity. One cannot infer calibration simply from the names of the representations.
Is uncertainty from the model the same thing as information from the observations?

No. The posterior reflects both the observations and the assumptions used to model conductivity and flux. In a weakly identifiable direction, assumptions can have a particularly strong influence because the observations provide limited discrimination. It is important not to interpret all posterior precision as precision supplied by the temperature observations.
What exactly does MCMC contribute to maintaining calibration?

Joint MCMC is a means of approximating the joint posterior, including relationships between the conductivity and flux unknowns. It can help carry that dependence through to reported intervals rather than dropping it during inference. It cannot create information that is absent from sparse observations, and even an accurately sampled posterior does not automatically imply that its intervals achieve a desired coverage rate.
Then what is the distinction between a posterior interval and a calibrated interval?

A posterior interval summarizes uncertainty under the specified Bayesian model, conditional on the observations. Calling intervals calibrated adds a performance claim: their stated coverage should correspond to how often they contain the relevant true quantity under the conditions being assessed. An interval can be correctly calculated from a posterior while that additional coverage claim remains unestablished.
Does near-collinearity make calibration impossible?

Not as a general rule. It makes separate inference about conductivity and flux more demanding and may require the intervals to acknowledge substantial uncertainty. Whether calibrated intervals are attainable depends on how well the uncertainty represented by the inference matches the circumstances being assessed. Near-collinearity is a reason to scrutinize coverage, not proof that coverage must fail.
Could I force calibration by making both intervals extremely broad?

Broadening intervals can increase how often they contain the true quantities, but it does not by itself establish the requested calibration. An interval can also be overly broad relative to its stated coverage level. The aim is to represent uncertainty appropriately, not merely to avoid excluding possible values at any cost.
The earlier goal calls for 90% interval coverage within five percentage points. Does the question ask how to establish that for both unknowns in the near-collinear case?

Yes, that is a concrete way to read “calibrated” in the context of the stated goal: the conductivity and flux intervals each have a 90% coverage target with a five-percentage-point tolerance across identifiability regimes. The near-collinear case probes the difficult part of that aim, where the sparse observations provide limited information for separating the unknowns. Nothing in the question reports that the target has been achieved.
If conductivity intervals have acceptable coverage but flux intervals do not, would the question be answered?

No. It explicitly asks about maintaining calibrated intervals for both conductivity and flux. The shared sensitivity is precisely why examining only one of them would miss part of the issue: uncertainty about the flux and uncertainty about conductivity are linked in the joint inference.
Does “joint” mean that the coverage target must refer to both intervals containing their true values at the same time?

Not necessarily. “Joint posterior” describes how conductivity and flux are inferred together and how their dependence is represented. The stated coverage requirement names intervals for each quantity; it does not specify a simultaneous-coverage criterion for both at once. Those are distinct notions, so one should not silently replace the stated requirement with the stronger one.
What if the posterior shows a narrow range for one unknown and a broad range for the other?

That pattern is not automatically inconsistent with joint inference. The observations and model might constrain the two differently. The question is whether each reported interval appropriately reflects uncertainty about its own quantity, including uncertainty propagated through the other, rather than whether the intervals have matching widths.
Is the main point that joint inference solves collinearity, or that it can express the uncertainty collinearity creates?

The latter. Joint inference provides a way to express dependence and unresolved trade-offs between conductivity and flux. It does not, by itself, separate effects that the sparse temperature observations leave nearly indistinguishable. The open question is whether the resulting intervals preserve that uncertainty well enough to be calibrated.
How would you state the unresolved issue without claiming a result?

The unresolved issue is whether a joint posterior for spatial conductivity and unknown boundary flux can yield reliably calibrated intervals for both when sparse temperature observations give nearly collinear sensitivity to the two. It asks whether the inference represents their ambiguity faithfully; it does not assert that the proposed Bayesian inversion already does so.

I have a hypothesis about the calibration question: marginalizing the Gaussian-process and flux-spline hyperparameters yields 85–95% coverage of 90% pointwise intervals across sensitivity-matrix condition numbers from 10 to 1000. How should I state it without making it sound like a result?

State it explicitly as a hypothesis: if uncertainty in both sets of hyperparameters is marginalized, the resulting 90% pointwise intervals for conductivity and boundary flux will have 85–95% coverage across sensitivity-matrix condition numbers of 10–1000. That makes the proposed outcome and its scope clear without saying the coverage has been observed.
What does marginalizing the hyperparameters mean in that sentence?

It means accounting for uncertainty in the Gaussian-process and flux-spline hyperparameters when forming the posterior intervals, rather than treating particular hyperparameter values as certain. The hypothesis is that carrying that uncertainty through to the intervals helps them attain the stated coverage. It does not specify which hyperparameters are involved or how the marginalization is computed.
Is the hypothesis about conductivity alone, since the Gaussian process describes log-conductivity?

No. It names hyperparameters associated with both the Gaussian-process representation and the flux-spline representation. In the context of the calibration question, the proposed coverage concerns pointwise intervals for conductivity and flux. It should not be shortened to a claim about conductivity intervals only.
Why mention hyperparameters for both representations?

Conductivity and flux are inferred jointly, and uncertainty in either representation can matter for the resulting intervals. The hypothesis specifically proposes marginalizing both sets of hyperparameters. Leaving either one out would change what is being proposed, even though the hypothesis does not claim how much each set contributes.
What does “90% pointwise intervals” mean here?

It refers to intervals stated at the 90% level for each individual point at which a quantity is considered. “Pointwise” distinguishes those intervals from a single band intended to cover an entire conductivity field or flux function simultaneously. The hypothesis concerns coverage of the pointwise intervals, not simultaneous coverage of every point.
So the 85–95% figure is not the nominal interval level?

Correct. The intervals are nominally 90% intervals. The hypothesized coverage is between 85% and 95%, meaning within five percentage points of that 90% level. The two percentages have different roles: one labels the intervals, and the other gives the proposed range for their coverage.
Could I say marginalization guarantees that range?

No. “Yields 85–95% coverage” is the content of the hypothesis, not an established guarantee. Marginalizing hyperparameters is the proposed feature of the inference; whether the resulting intervals actually attain that coverage across the stated condition-number range remains the question the hypothesis addresses.
How do the condition numbers relate to the earlier concern about nearly collinear sensitivities?

The condition number characterizes how unevenly the sensitivity matrix responds in different directions. Larger condition numbers can indicate greater difficulty separating changes in conductivity from changes in flux through the available observations. The range 10–1000 gives the scope over which the coverage hypothesis is proposed; it does not assert that every case in that range has identical ambiguity.
Does including 1000 mean the hypothesis assumes conductivity and flux are exactly nonidentifiable there?

No. A condition number of 1000 does not, by itself, assert exact nonidentifiability. The hypothesis spans sensitivity matrices with condition numbers from 10 to 1000, including cases where separation of effects may be difficult. It does not identify a particular condition number at which the two unknowns become exactly indistinguishable.
Should “across 10–1000” be read as coverage at only one representative condition number?

No; that would lose the stated range. The hypothesis concerns coverage across sensitivity-matrix condition numbers of 10–1000, rather than solely at one chosen value. It does not, however, specify an assessment procedure or precisely how coverage would be summarized within that range.
Does it say coverage must be exactly 90% at every condition number?

No. The proposed coverage range is 85–95% for nominal 90% pointwise intervals. The hypothesis also does not specify a condition-number-by-condition-number reporting rule, so it is best to retain its stated scope and tolerance without adding a stricter requirement of exactly 90% everywhere.
If a 90% interval had 95% coverage, would that be inside the hypothesized range?
Yes. Both endpoints, 85% and 95%, fall within the stated range as written. That is a statement about the numerical hypothesis, not evidence that any interval has attained either endpoint.
Is this hypothesis also a claim about reconstruction error compared with known boundary flux?

No. This hypothesis concerns coverage of 90% pointwise intervals after marginalizing Gaussian-process and flux-spline hyperparameters, across sensitivity-matrix condition numbers of 10–1000. It does not make a reconstruction-error claim or establish a comparison with the known-flux case.
Would posterior intervals computed after fixing hyperparameters count as the same hypothesis?

No. Fixing the hyperparameters would omit the marginalization named in the hypothesis. Both approaches might produce posterior intervals, but this particular proposed coverage range is attributed to intervals that account for uncertainty in the Gaussian-process and flux-spline hyperparameters.
Can I explain the idea as uncertainty in model flexibility being carried into uncertainty about conductivity and flux?

That is a reasonable conceptual explanation, provided it does not imply that any specific flexibility settings or their effects have been established. The key idea is to carry uncertainty about the two representations' hyperparameters into the reported pointwise intervals, rather than presenting intervals conditional on fixed settings as though those settings were known.
Does marginalizing those hyperparameters resolve the near-collinearity itself?

No. It accounts for an additional source of uncertainty within the proposed joint inference; it does not change the fact that sparse temperature observations may respond similarly to changes in conductivity and flux. The hypothesis is that the resulting intervals have 85–95% coverage despite that sensitivity issue across the specified condition-number range, not that marginalization removes the issue.
What would be the most careful short formulation?

“We hypothesize that marginalizing Gaussian-process and flux-spline hyperparameters yields 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% pointwise conductivity and boundary-flux intervals across sensitivity-matrix condition numbers of 10–1000.” That preserves the numerical range, the pointwise nature of the intervals, both unknowns, and the fact that the statement is a hypothesis.
How would we plan to examine whether the joint intervals stay calibrated when conductivity and flux have similar effects on sparse temperature observations?

The plan is to simulate heat fields across sensitivity-matrix condition numbers from 10 to 1000. Using those simulations, we would assess coverage of intervals from hyperparameter-marginalized MCMC. We would also compare conductivity reconstruction error in identifiable joint-recovery cases against a known-flux inversion. These are planned comparisons, not reported results.
Why use a range of condition numbers rather than just one difficult case?

The range lets the planned assessment address varying degrees of difficulty in distinguishing the effects of conductivity and boundary flux. It also matches the stated scope of the coverage hypothesis: condition numbers from 10 to 1000. The plan does not specify particular condition numbers within that range or how many simulated heat fields would be used.
Does a condition number of 1000 mean we will simulate an exactly nonidentifiable problem?

Not necessarily. A larger condition number can signal a more difficult sensitivity relationship, but the plan does not equate 1000 with exact nonidentifiability. The stated action is to simulate heat fields across the 10–1000 range and examine how inference performs there.
What exactly are we checking in the coverage comparison?

We would check how often the relevant intervals contain the simulated conductivity and flux quantities they are intended to cover. The proposed intervals come from MCMC with the Gaussian-process and flux-spline hyperparameters marginalized. In the established hypothesis, these are nominal 90% pointwise intervals, with 85–95% coverage hypothesized across the condition-number range. The plan sets up an assessment of that claim; it does not say the claim holds.
Why does the plan specify hyperparameter-marginalized MCMC rather than just MCMC?

Because marginalizing those hyperparameters is part of the inference whose coverage is in question. The comparison should concern intervals that carry uncertainty in both the Gaussian-process and flux-spline hyperparameters through the joint posterior. Merely saying “MCMC” would leave open whether those hyperparameters had instead been treated as fixed.
Are we comparing coverage only for conductivity?

No. The coverage question concerns intervals for both conductivity and the unknown boundary flux. The separate reconstruction-error comparison in this plan is specifically about conductivity. Keeping those two assessments distinct avoids turning a conductivity-error comparison into an unstated flux-error requirement.
Where does the known-flux inversion enter?

It is the reference for the planned conductivity reconstruction-error comparison in cases where joint recovery is identifiable. The plan asks how conductivity error under joint inference compares with conductivity error when the boundary flux is known. It does not propose treating flux as known in the joint inference whose interval coverage is being assessed.
Should we compare conductivity error against that reference at every condition number from 10 to 1000?

The plan specifies the known-flux conductivity-error comparison for identifiable joint-recovery cases. It does not extend that error comparison to cases where joint recovery is nonidentifiable. Simulating across 10–1000 supports examination of the condition-number range, while the identifiable-case condition limits where this particular error comparison applies.
Does the plan say which condition numbers count as identifiable?

No. It calls for an identifiable-case comparison but does not define an identifiability threshold or assign particular condition numbers to that category. We should not infer a cutoff from the endpoints of the simulated range.
How does the within-20% target fit into the comparison?

It supplies the established criterion for the identifiable-case conductivity result: conductivity reconstruction error under joint recovery should be within 20% of the known-flux conductivity reconstruction error. The plan would make that comparison possible, but it does not report either error or say that the criterion has been met.
Is the known-flux inversion also the benchmark for whether the unknown-flux intervals have calibrated coverage?

The known-flux inversion is named as the reference for identifiable-case conductivity reconstruction error. For interval coverage, the issue is whether the hyperparameter-marginalized MCMC intervals for conductivity and flux cover their corresponding quantities at the intended rate across the simulated condition-number range. The plan does not specify a known-flux coverage benchmark for the unknown flux.
What does simulating heat fields give us that the sparse observations alone do not?

For the planned assessment, simulation provides heat fields under which the conductivity and flux being inferred are available for comparison with the resulting intervals and reconstruction. That makes coverage and reconstruction error assessable. The plan does not specify the simulation model's detailed settings or claim that any simulations have already been run.
Would one heat field be enough to establish 90% coverage?

A single instance can show whether a particular interval contains its corresponding value, but coverage is about a rate across assessed instances. The plan says to simulate heat fields across condition numbers 10–1000; it does not specify a number of simulations or a coverage-estimation procedure. Those details should not be filled in as though they were already decided.
Could we interpret an interval that gets wider at a higher condition number as a failure?

Width alone would not establish failure. If conductivity and flux become harder to distinguish, wider intervals may reflect the increased uncertainty. The planned coverage assessment concerns whether the intervals contain the relevant values at an appropriate rate, not whether their widths stay constant across condition numbers. No interval-width criterion is stated.
What if the intervals have the desired coverage but the identifiable-case conductivity error differs substantially from known-flux inversion?

That would address the two assessments differently: interval coverage concerns reported uncertainty for conductivity and flux, while the known-flux comparison concerns identifiable-case conductivity reconstruction error. The plan calls for both, so a coverage finding alone would not settle the error comparison. The plan itself does not predict either finding.
And a close match in conductivity error would not establish flux interval coverage?

Correct. A close conductivity-error comparison against known-flux inversion would not show how often the flux intervals contain the corresponding flux values. The coverage assessment still needs to address the MCMC intervals for both unknowns across the stated condition-number range.
Can I describe the plan as testing whether marginalizing hyperparameters fixes near-collinear sensitivities?

That would overstate what marginalization is proposed to do. The plan assesses whether intervals from hyperparameter-marginalized MCMC maintain appropriate coverage when the sensitivity relationship varies across condition numbers 10–1000. It does not propose that marginalization changes the sensitivities or removes ambiguity between conductivity and flux.
Does the plan commit to a particular error measure, spline specification, or Gaussian-process kernel?

No. It names the simulated condition-number range, the hyperparameter-marginalized MCMC coverage assessment, and the identifiable-case conductivity-error comparison with known-flux inversion. It leaves the particular reconstruction-error measure and those modeling specifications unstated.
How can I phrase the whole plan without implying the simulations or comparisons have already happened?

“We plan to simulate heat fields with sensitivity-matrix condition numbers from 10 to 1000, assess coverage of conductivity and flux intervals from hyperparameter-marginalized MCMC, and compare identifiable-case conductivity reconstruction error with known-flux inversion.” That keeps the range and the two assessments explicit while leaving their outcomes open.
What is the concrete trial activity for assessing the intervals and reconstruction error?

Run 200 synthetic heat-equation trials per condition-number bin across the 10–1000 range. In those trials, measure interval coverage for both conductivity and boundary flux, and measure conductivity RMSE relative to a known-flux inversion. That specifies the activity and its measurements; it does not report any outcomes.
Is it 200 trials total, divided among the bins?

No. The specified count is 200 synthetic heat-equation trials *per condition-number bin*. The activity does not state how many bins there are or where their boundaries fall, so it does not imply a total trial count.
What does binning by condition number contribute?

It allows the measurements to be considered across the specified sensitivity-matrix condition-number range of 10–1000, rather than only as one undifferentiated assessment. That matters because the question concerns how interval coverage behaves as conductivity and flux become harder to distinguish from sparse temperature observations. No particular bin boundaries are specified.
Are the conductivity and flux coverage measurements separate?

Yes. The activity calls for measuring coverage for conductivity intervals and for flux intervals. A result for one would not stand in for the other. The established hypothesis concerns 90% pointwise intervals having 85–95% coverage across the condition-number range, but this activity does not yet say what coverage either set of intervals achieves.
What would coverage mean within one of these bins?

Conceptually, it is the proportion of assessed intervals that contain the corresponding quantity in the synthetic trials assigned to that bin. The 200-trial count makes a within-bin assessment possible. The activity does not specify a particular way to aggregate pointwise coverage within or across trials, so that detail should remain open.
Does a measured coverage rate from 200 trials become the true coverage rate?

No. A rate measured from a finite set of synthetic trials is an estimate from those trials. The activity specifies 200 trials per bin, not certainty about the underlying coverage rate. It also does not provide any measured rate yet.
Should the intervals be described as 90% intervals even before coverage is measured?

Yes, as a description of their nominal level in the hypothesis: they are 90% pointwise intervals. The trial activity measures how often the conductivity and flux intervals actually contain the corresponding synthetic quantities. Calling an interval nominally 90% does not assert that its measured coverage is 90%.
How does the known-flux comparison differ from the coverage measurements?

Coverage asks whether the reported conductivity and flux intervals contain the corresponding quantities. The known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE measures reconstruction error for conductivity against the known-flux inversion as a reference. It is an error comparison for conductivity, not a coverage measurement for either unknown.
Is the activity asking for flux RMSE relative to known flux too?

No. It specifies conductivity/flux *interval coverage* and known-flux-relative *conductivity RMSE*. It does not specify a flux RMSE comparison. The word “flux” in the coverage measurement should not be extended to the RMSE measurement.
Why say “relative to known-flux inversion” instead of giving an RMSE threshold here?

The activity identifies what to measure: conductivity RMSE in relation to the known-flux reference. The established goal provides the comparison of within 20% when joint recovery is identifiable. This activity does not report RMSE values or say whether that comparison is satisfied.
Would that within-20% comparison apply to every bin?

The earlier condition on that comparison is that joint recovery be identifiable. The activity spans condition-number bins from 10 to 1000, but it does not label particular bins as identifiable or specify an identifiability cutoff. So the 20% criterion should not be assigned automatically to every bin.
Does a high condition number automatically identify which trials are nonidentifiable?

No. The condition number helps characterize the sensitivity relationship, but this activity does not define a condition-number threshold for identifiability. It specifies a range to assess and a count of trials per bin, not a rule that classifies individual trials.
Are these trials observations from an actual heat system?

They are specified as *synthetic heat-equation trials*. That permits comparing inferred quantities and intervals with the quantities used in the trials. The activity does not describe an observational dataset or claim that any physical-system measurements have been collected.
Does “run 200” mean we can discuss the findings as though the trials are complete?

No. It states the trial activity to carry out. Without reported measurements, we cannot say whether the intervals achieve 85–95% coverage, whether conductivity RMSE is within 20% of the known-flux reference in identifiable cases, or how either measure varies across bins.
